pl-l2d33c1-d1e108.summary: Asks whether the sins of earlier ancestors pass to infants as Adam's sin did to all born carnally, and if so, whether of all from Adam on or only some.

pl-l2d33c1-d1e111.summary: States that Augustine in the Enchiridion speaks ambiguously, seeming to approve that ancestors' sins are imputed to infants, not of all since Adam, lest they be crushed by an unbearable burden, but only up to the fourth generation, as in 'visiting the iniquities of the fathers to the third and fourth generation,' by the moderation of divine mercy.
claims: Augustine seems to limit imputation to four generations.

pl-l2d33c1-d1e114.summary: Reports the supporting argument: infants are baptized for the remission of sins, in the plural, and David, born of lawful marriage, says he was conceived in iniquities and sins, not in iniquity or sin; so more than the one original sin, both the several sins in Adam's sin and other ancestral sins, are imputed to infants.
claims: The plural is taken to imply several imputed sins.

pl-l2d33c1.summary: Asks whether the sins of earlier ancestors pass to infants as Adam's did, and if so, whether all from Adam onward or only some. Augustine in the Enchiridion speaks ambiguously, seeming to approve that the sins of ancestors up to the fourth generation are imputed, by God's mitigating mercy (Exod 20:5), not all, lest infants bear an unbearable burden. Supporters note that infants are baptized 'for the remission of sins,' plural, and David says he was conceived 'in iniquities' and 'in sins.'
claims: Whether ancestors' sins besides Adam's pass to infants must be asked.
Augustine seems to allow imputation of ancestors' sins to the fourth generation.
Some argue from the plurals 'sins' and 'iniquities' that several sins are imputed to infants.
